utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the registrar would call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear standing in for Ms. Haslund who is ill, unfortunately, and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. Paterson and Dr. Staker, if Your Honours please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Deyan Brashich appearing for the defendant Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic acting on behalf of Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good afternoon. I am Borislav Pisarevic, acting on behalf of Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Branislav Avramovic, representing Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This hearing is to deal with various outstanding motions. I was not present on the hearing last week, but as I understand it, the following matters are outstanding: Firstly, there was a motion which was heard -- and I, of course, read the transcript -- concerning an alleged conflict of interest in counsel representing Mr. Simo Zaric, that is, Mr. Pisarevic. That matter was fully argued, but the Trial Chamber agreed to hear any representations which any of the accused wish to make, and we will hear those to start with. There are then two motions on behalf of

utterances.speaker: MR. TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Firstly, a motion in relation to an evidentiary hearing which he applies for in relation to his arrest, and then there is a motion to sever counts. Those matters were not heard on the last occasion because a Bench of three, it was thought, should hear it. Those are the matters which are outstanding, as I understand it. When we have concluded those, I hope that there will be time before we finish at about half past five to have a Status Conference so that we can see what progress is being made in this case. Very well. Are there any other matters before we go into those motions? Anybody want to raise anything? Very well. I am going to turn to the accused, and as I have already said, the Trial Chamber, on the last occasion, did agree to hear any representations which any of you may want to make on this topic. Mr. Brashich, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On behalf of Mr. Todorovic, I will make a representation that I have fully discussed the conflict issue, and it is the position of the accused Todorovic that it does not intend to call Mr. Pisarevic either on its case in chief or in rebuttal, and I speak for my client, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as the other accused who are present, or indeed representing the absent accused, I shall ask if there is anything that they would like to say or anything additional they would like to say through their counsel. Now, Mr. Pisarevic, does Mr. Zaric wish to say something about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, certainly Mr. Zaric would like to comment as it has to do with his right of choice of Defence counsel, and he would like to acquaint the Trial Chamber with his views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zaric, we will hear from you. THE ACCUSED ZARIC: (Interpretation) Mr. President, Your Honours, there is no need for me to waste words in discussing to what extent my rights would be called in question if the position of my attorney, Mr. Pisarevic -- if he were prevented from defending me in this already final pre-trial stage, and I hope that the trial itself will begin shortly. Of course, I have still not lost hope that the gentlemen from the Prosecution who have certainly dealt in-depth into the situation in wartime Samac will propose to the Trial Chamber that the indictment be quashed and I be released. That would be an honourable act on their part. But awaiting such a move on the part of the Prosecution -- I just wish to tell Your Honours that I chose Mr. Pisarevic as my attorney for two main reasons: First, because, as a man, I have full trust in him in every respect and I hope that there is no need for me to elaborate on that; and, secondly, because in addition to his professional ability and his reputation as an attorney in Samac and broader, I respect him as a man who spent the whole wartime period in Samac, who has authentic knowledge of the situation in the town and around it at the time, and who went through this hell together with me, and I am deeply confident that in addition to his obligations towards me as a client, which cannot be called in question, Mr. Pisarevic will also be of great value to this Trial Chamber as a participant in those events and as an honourable and honest individual. Therefore, as a person well-versed in the conditions in the town of Samac in the period under consideration in this trial and on the basis of insight into the Prosecution's documents which has drawn attention to the possibility of a conflict of interest, I wish to point out that between me, as the accused, and Mr. Pisarevic, as my Defence counsel, in no stage of the proceedings can a conflict of interest occur. I also take the liberty to say that in the case of the other co-accused and the Prosecution too, this cannot be questioned if the substance of the problem is viewed rather than the marginal effect of certain relevant facts. Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Now, does anybody else want to say anything? Mr. Tadic, do you want to say anything? Yes, Mr. Tadic? THE ACCUSED TADIC: (Interpretation) Your Honours, my position too is that between me and Mr. Zaric in this trial, there would be no conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, as we all know, Mr. Milan Simic, my client, is not here present today, but I have briefed him on all the details linked to the Prosecution motion, and I would like to convey his position. The Defence of Mr. Simic, and he in person, will not call Mr. Pisarevic as a witness in this case. The position of Mr. Milan Simic is, furthermore, that should Mr. Pisarevic appear as a witness under any circumstances, his Defence reserves the right to examine him as a witness. That is the position of Mr. Milan Simic and his Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will move on next to the other motions. It would seem convenient to deal, first of all, with the motion in relation to an evidentiary hearing. We have received, in relation to that, the motion and a response, both dated last month, and we have also received a memorandum of law which strictly is outside the normal pleadings, but if Mr. Brashich wants us to consider it, then he can apply for us to do so. You could take it, as I say, that we have read those documents, but we will hear submissions on anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence, at this present juncture, is placed in a very difficult position. In order to move this Court with a request that the indictment be dismissed, quashed, and for a further order that my client be returned to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in order to establish a prima facie case, I would have to put before this Court, without a limiting order, testimony by Mr. Todorovic which would open the door to cross-examination on other wide-ranging subjects. Based on that consideration, I chose to move this Trial Chamber for an evidentiary hearing to ascertain the nature of the arrest and apprehension of my client and then for a further order to make the motion to dismiss and for an order, they can call it repatriation, to a country of his refuge. In the original motion, I had alleged and offered, at least as some evidence, newspaper reports as to my client's abduction. The Prosecutor saw fit to go at great lengths that this was not a prima facie case, and I again returned back to the quandary that the Defence is or was placed initially when it made the motion. However, once the Defence has raised an illegal abduction, violation of sovereign laws, I believe that the Trial Chamber should take the position that the burden has shifted to the Prosecution. The Prosecution now has the burden to justify the abduction, if there was one, or if there was not one, to come forward and say, "Mr. Todorovic was found in a cafe in Dusseldorf, recognised by a German police officer, arrested, read his rights, and thereafter the machinations of removing him to the United Nations' detention facility took place, and here he is now before this court in a lawful and proper way. The burden shifts even further to the Prosecution, or perhaps it shifts back to the Defence, that I have the right to establish what participation, if any, agents, servants, or employees of the Prosecution participated in this abduction or whether some other agents of the United Nations, surrogates thereof, acting in concert, did that, which would elevate the abduction to state action. I believe that another Trial Chamber in this very court has followed that procedure, and that is the case of the Prosecution against Slavko Dokmanovic, IT-95-13a-PT, where just such an evidentiary hearing was held. Now, I had made an offer of proof in my memorandum of law that should this Court grant a motion in limine and allow the defendant to testify without waiving any of his other rights, solely on the issue of arrest, abduction, kidnapping, and other violations of law which occurred, he would testify that he was on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in September 1998. He will testify that four individuals came to the premises where he was living with weapons and, under threat of force, took him from his place of residence, blindfolded him, put him into a car, and drove him across the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a telephone call was made, that thereafter, while blindfolded, he was taken across the River Drina, walked through the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that a walkie-talkie telephone call was made, that a helicopter appeared within 10 or 15 minutes, that he was thrown blindfolded into the helicopter and then taken to an armed forces base. This all happened in two or three hours. It raises the issue of the Prosecution's involvement in this abduction or people acting on behalf of the Prosecution, and if these were the traditional bounty hunters of the Wild West, whether or not the Prosecution had, in fact, paid for the commission of crimes under the laws of the Republic of Yugoslavia or under the laws of the Republic of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then in my memorandum of law, because this is a subject that has been debated at great length and many opinions and decisions made by various jurisdictions, I asked further leave to fully brief the issues. I brought to the Court's attention a law review article of Jiaming Shen, which appeared in the Denver Journal of International Law and Policy, which discusses the illegal abduction/detention, both by state agencies and by private individuals. At this present time, Your Honour, I'm not in a position, unless I get the evidentiary hearing, whether to address the issues that I have raised solely as to the bounty hunter, the totally private individual, and thereafter the adoption, the concurrence, the approval of the Prosecution of such illegal acts or, on the other hand, as I suspect based on the time factors and how this whole abduction took place, that I will be in a position to further argue "actual state," and I'm putting that in quotes and I'm using the word "state" as it appears in various decisions and treaties, the state action of the Prosecutor here as, in fact, being raised to a higher level, and not only an initial violation of local laws and thereafter that violation rising to international violations of law, to an immediate finding that there was a violation of international law by a state, in this instance, a self-contained state called the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia. As is noted in various articles and treaties, there really is one case in point, and that's the Eichmann case where alleged private individuals spirited Eichmann to Israel for trial. The authorities all concur that it was the uniqueness, the gross crimes committed by Eichmann during the Second World War, that makes Eichmann's case not to be followed in a situation such as this. I am mindful of the decisions in my country, the United States, including the last decision of the Supreme Court. I submit, Your Honour, that the standards that a sovereign nation applies are not the standard that this International Tribunal should apply. This is an International Tribunal, and if there is international law, then this Tribunal perforce must pay respect and do all in its power to uphold international law, and if international law has been breached, as the cases suggest, there is only one appropriate decision that this Court can make, to free Mr. Todorovic, to order his forthwith return to the former Yugoslavia, to allow thereafter whatever the law, including the Statutes of this Tribunal, provide, and if someone had violated the law, to apply either corrective measures or punitive measures, and for an example, I note, in reading one of this Court's decisions, that apparently perjury occurred, and it's being pursued by the Prosecutor's office or some other branch of this Tribunal because its very existence is threatened by breaches of law such as perjury or, in this instance, by illegal criminal acts. So I would again urge that I get an evidentiary hearing, that the Prosecutor be forced to disclose the names of all participants who had, in any way, dealt with the arrest and abduction of my client, and then leave it for me to make an appropriate motion. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, let me just follow your final point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me follow your final point. You ask for an evidentiary hearing, and at that hearing, you're asking that your client should give evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, with a motion in limine where his testifying would not open the door, except to the issue of abduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then you say that there should be an order to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: For discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What, all details that they know about the arrest; is that what you're asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The names of the witnesses, the participants, if there are any reports which have been made by the United Nations forces or who had acted either prior to the abduction, during the abduction, or at the tail end of the action so that I can interview them, and then I can either show, and again I put this in quotes "private action" or, in the alternative, state action and lay that at the doorstep of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I begin, I will tell the interpreters that I will make every effort to speak slowly today. I'm reminded of that every time, and I will make a best effort today. The Prosecution submits that the accused's motion regarding his arrest is, first of all, not timely, that it should be dismissed in limine on the ground that it discloses no prima facie basis for any judicial inquiry, that even if the motion were considered on its merits, it should be denied in its entirety as the relevant facts, even if proved, would not constitute a violation of the fundamental rights of the accused, and finally, the accused has failed to make a sufficient legal showing to warrant the remedies that he has requested. We would begin by noting, as we have in response to all the other motions filed by Mr. Brashich on behalf of Mr. Todorovic, that the motion was not brought in a timely manner. It was not filed initially by the date set in the scheduling order, and no good cause was shown for the late filing. As Your Honour noted, Mr. Brashich has, indeed, since then now filed another memorandum, again outside the scheduling order. It's our contention that all parties must respect the orders of the Trial Chamber and that, again, the Defence has made no good cause showing for why this motion was filed late, and he should be precluded from filing the instant motion. In regard to timeliness, however, we feel there's an even more egregious error on the part of the Defence, and that is that they failed to bring this motion before the Court at the earliest opportunity. Since the subject of the motion deals with the alleged non-compliance with the Rules, pursuant to Rule 5(b), this motion should have been brought at the earliest opportunity. If, as the Defence alleges, this is such a serious violation of the defendant's rights that it warrants dismissal of the indictment and immediate release of the defendant, then arguably this motion should have been filed within the first 24 hours after the defendant appeared here before the Tribunal. Failure to do so belies the Defence argument as to the serious nature of the alleged offences committed in taking the defendant into custody. At his first appearance before this Chamber on the 30th of September, 1998, the defendant informed the Court that he had allegedly been taken from his hiding place, which Mr. Brashich refers to as his country of refuge, and that he had allegedly been taken from that hiding place in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and transported to Bosnia where his arrest was affected, and on the same occasion, the Defence counsel at the time, Mr. Neskovic, commented on the record about the circumstances of the arrest. While it is true that the OTP amended the indictment after the 30th of September and that amendment then triggered new periods in which to file motions, the amendment of the indictment in no way whatsoever changed the alleged facts on which the defendant is claiming today to challenge the legality of his arrest nor can it be an excuse that the current Defence counsel, Mr. Brashich, replaced the original Defence counsel, Mr. Neskovic, in December. That change also did not in any way affect either Defence attorney's ability to file this motion in a timely manner. The Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal are established to guarantee a fair trial for all the parties, the Defence and the Prosecution. The Court should not allow late filings and disregard for the Rules, especially without a request to file the motions late or any showing of good cause. Even if Your Honours are not persuaded by the timeliness argument, the accused's motion does not establish a prima facie basis for judicial inquiry. Despite what Mr. Brashich says, the onus is on the accused as the moving party to satisfy the Trial Chamber that there is a serious question of law to be considered. Without such a showing, the lawfulness of the detention of the accused and the regularity of the conduct of the Tribunal staff must be presumed. In order to make a prima facie showing, the accused must first state with specific particularity the facts which give rise to the illegality. Second, present arguable, legal reasons why the facts alleged by the Defence, if proved, would render the accused's arrest or detention unlawful, and finally must provide the Trial Chamber with sufficient factual material to establish a prima facie basis for the accused's contention. The motion before the Court contains no statement of the accused's version of the facts nor any firsthand allegation of fact at all. Mr. Brashich today has argued that he could not present such a version of the defendant's facts without the defendant testifying at the hearing, but the Prosecution sees no reason why an affidavit could not have been prepared and submitted to this Court limited strictly to the facts of his arrested as alleged by Mr. Todorovic. The Defence has also attempted to bolster its original argument by means of an offer of proof filed just this past Monday, but that offer of proof sheds no new light on the facts or the original legal arguments. In its original motion, the Defence merely referred to published reports that the accused was allegedly illegally abducted from the territory of the FRY. The attachment to the motion appears to be no more than a copy of the first two pages of a three-page message which was posted by a private individual on an e-mail bulletin board, and the message contains what purports to be the text of a single report from The Times newspaper of London. The attachment is thus, at best, a source of fourth-hand or fifth-hand hearsay. Mere reference to this quadruple or quintuple hearsay, which fails to even identify the original sources, accompanied by the accused's own failure to give an account of his own of the facts, is clearly insufficient to establish a factual basis on which to consider the motion. It is particularly noteworthy that the Defence motion contains no reference to any conduct whatsoever on the part of the Prosecutor. The Defence presents no facts to support the contention that the Prosecutor, in some way, acted in concert with SFOR or anything else in relation to any actions which may have been carried out in regard to the defendant's arrest in the territory of the FRY. Based on the motion submitted by the Defence, he asked this Court, simply by referring to a posting on an e-mail bulletin board, whose basis is multiple levels of hearsay, to shift the burden to the Prosecution to justify the legality of the defendant's arrest and detention, and he then asks the Trial Chamber to undertake an open-ended inquiry into the surrounding circumstances of the defendant's seizure, an undertaking which would amount to nothing more than a fishing expedition on the part of the Defence. The Defence submission manifestly fails to satisfy the requirements, (1) to state, with sufficient particularity, the facts, and (2) to provide the Trial Chamber with sufficient factual material to establish a prima facie basis for the accused's contention. Most significantly, as we will detail in the remainder of our argument, the accused fails to present any arguable legal reasons why the facts as alleged by the Defence, even if proved, would render the accused's arrest or detention unlawful. This Trial Chamber should insist that the Defence present it with sufficient factual material to establish a prima facie basis for the accused's contention, and having failed to do so, this motion should be dismissed in limine on the ground that it discloses no serious question of law to be examined. While we believe we have already provided the Trial Chamber with several reasons to deny the Defendant's motion, even if the illegality or irregularity suggested in the accused's motion were true, which we do not concede, that would not justify the relief being sought. In beginning to consider the subject of the Defence's contentions, we would first remind the Chamber of the limited relationship that the Tribunal has with those who act as our so-called police force, and that we stress the fact that the Office of the Prosecutor had no involvement in any alleged activity relating to the accused's removal from the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Before addressing those points, let me remind the Court of the facts in regard to Mr. Todorovic. Mr. Todorovic was indicted on the 21st of July, 1995, and arrest warrants were signed the same day and served on the authorities of Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Todorovic was indicted for multiple counts of murder, wilful killing, wilfully causing great suffering, cruel treatment, inhumane acts, inhuman treatment, humiliating and degrading treatment, rape, and torture. The indictment was made public and was widely reported in the media, including in the former Yugoslavia. Todorovic had known for over three years that he was wanted by the ICTY. During those three years, he was living in Republika Srpska and was known to spend time in Pale. Despite having been served with a copy of the arrest warrant on the 24th of July, 1995, the government authorities of Republika Srpska refused to arrest him and turn him over to the ICTY. He continued to elude capture, and once it became clear SFOR was actively arresting persons in Republika Srpska, Mr. Todorovic moved to the FRY where he knew the government was also refusing to arrest and turn over persons indicted by the ICTY. Thus we are discussing an indicted war criminal who has intentionally hidden himself for three years from any authorities who would or could arrest him. As a war criminal, he is charged with some of the most serious criminal offences that exist in international law. Taking all that into consideration, we remind the Court at the start that the Tribunal is a unique international organisation created pursuant to Chapter 7 of the U.N. Charter. It is not a state and it cannot be equated with a state. In its motion, the Defence alleges that the accused was forcibly abducted from the FRY and taken to Bosnia. Even if that were true, which we in no way concede, a review of the case law applicable to incidents of alleged forcible abductions shows that the argument made against such activity is based on the premise that permitting such actions would taint the whole justice process if the police and Prosecution authorities of the forum state were themselves involved in the breaches of the same system of criminal law that they are responsible for enforcing against others. None of these cases suggest, as is the analogous situation here, that a court should decline to exercise jurisdiction over a defendant in circumstances where the authorities of the forum state, or in this case the forum tribunal, have acted with propriety, merely because the authorities of another state have acted irregularly. Indeed, the process of justice would be defeated if a prosecution were required to be stopped whenever there was improper conduct on the part of agents of another state, especially when the authorities of the forum state can exercise no control and have no power of sanction. This has been noted by other Trial Chambers. The Tribunal lacks any police or other enforcement agency of its own and must rely upon the cooperation of states for the arrest and delivery of indictees. Since the Tribunal has to rely on the military and police forces of other states to arrest our indictees, we are certainly not in a position to exercise operational control over the state agents who provide that support nor should we seek to exercise such control, since to do so would overstep the bounds of our role as Prosecutors and Judges. Policing matters should be left to those professionals who are in a position to assess the situation and make the proper decisions regarding operational matters. In addition to having no control over SFOR or any private individuals who might have been involved in the arrest of Mr. Todorovic, the Office of the Prosecutor had no prior information of any proposed operation to secure the arrest of the accused. The first knowledge that the Office of the Prosecutor had of the matter was on the 27th of September, 1998, when it was informed by SFOR, pursuant to established procedures and Rule 57, that SFOR had the accused in custody in northern Bosnia. Investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor immediately went to the Tuzla air base where they effected his arrest and followed all the procedures mandated by the Rules, including Rules 55, subsections E, F, and G. In light of these issues, we respectfully urge the Court to bear in mind the reality of the Tribunal's unique situation as well as the reality of Mr. Todorovic's situation as you consider our arguments. Turning now to the substance of the Defence motion, the accused alleges that his fundamental rights were violated, but he fails to articulate what specific fundamental rights were violated, and even if true, why dismissal of the indictment is the only remedy available to the Court. Even if we were to assume for the sake of argument the following facts -- and I wish to stress for the Court, for everyone in the public gallery, and for the media, that we do not in any way concede these facts, we are assuming them only for the purposes of argument -- there is still no showing that the Defendant's fundamental rights were violated. Let us assume arguendo that the accused had been invited by the Tribunal, that the accused was in the FRY where he could be reasonably certain, from the past record of the authorities there, that he would be safe from arrest and beyond the reach of the Tribunal. Let us assume that the accused was taken forcibly and against his will from FRY territory by agents of a state or states other than the FRY and that the only arrest warrants relating to the accused that had been issued by the Tribunal were addressed to authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia, of which copies had been transmitted to SFOR. Let us assume that his forcible removal from the FRY was effected without the consent of the FRY authorities and constituted a violation of the sovereignty of the FRY under international law as well as a breach of the municipal law of the FRY, and, finally, let us assume that the accused was immediately transported within Bosnia and Herzegovina to a point of embarkation and flown to The Hague where he was taken to the Tribunal's detention unit. Despite this scenario, even if the Defendant were taken from the FRY against his will, this does not mean that any violation of a state sovereignty necessarily entitles an accused to a remedy. Most case law decisions on the issue of violations of sovereignty are premised on the fact that the removal of the accused from the other state involved a circumvention of applicable extradition procedures. But the Tribunal is not a foreign jurisdiction or a state, it is an international judicial body that enjoys world-wide jurisdiction over any accused anywhere in the world. A violation of state sovereignty is a violation of the rights of the relevant state. To be entitled to a remedy, the accused would need to establish that this violation of a state's sovereignty also constituted some violation of his own fundamental rights. Furthermore, as noted in the Blaskic case before this Tribunal, no state has a right to insist on any special protections such as those that arise in extradition scenarios, before handing an accused over to the Tribunal. In addressing an issue relating to an extradition matter, the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has held that the principle of speciality, a common protection for accused persons under extradition arrangements, has no counterpart in the case of an accused who is transferred by a national authority to the Tribunal. For all of the reasons I have just cited, there is clearly no violation of any rights of the Defendant under the laws of extradition. As noted, the Defendant has alleged that he was forcibly abducted from the FRY, but even if true, the facts of this case are entirely distinguishable from a case where an accused, who is subject to the protection of the laws of one country, is forcibly removed contrary to the laws protecting him into the jurisdiction of another country's legal system. An accused's right to security of the person does not confer a right to seek protection from the processes of the Tribunal by remaining in a country that the accused can competently expect will fail to fulfil its obligations of cooperation with the Tribunal. It would be legally inconsistent and against common sense if an individual right could be deducted from a state's reluctance or failure to comply with its international obligations. Such a doctrine might potentially encourage certain states, such as the FRY, to ensure that serious irregularities are committed in the arrest process before handing the accused to the Tribunal, being confident that after review, the indictment would be dismissed and the Defendant released because the Defendant's rights had been violated by the authorities in the FRY. Under that scenario, the states concerned could claim that they are fulfilling their obligation of cooperation while, at the same time, sabotaging the Prosecution because the Defendant's fundamental rights were violated by the irregularities in the process. As noted in the Dokmanovic case referred to by Mr. Brashich, pursuant to Rule 59 bis, once an arrest warrant has been transmitted to an international authority, an international body, or the OTP, the accused person named therein may be taken into custody without the involvement of the state in which he is located. If the FRY wanted to claim that there had been a violation of its sovereignty, and there is no indication of any relevant protest by the FRY, this would be a matter to be resolved between the states concerned in accordance with the international law principles of dispute settlement. It does not invoke a personal right on the part of the accused. Even in the Defence motion there is no suggestion that the rights of the accused under Rule 55 were not observed at the time of arrest by OTP personnel. We also note that the accused is now in the custody of the Tribunal, in apparent good health, and not suffering from any serious injury, because even if force was utilised, the force was reasonable under the circumstances as is permitted in all national arrest scenarios. Thus there are no grounds for dismissing the indictment due to irregularities in the process, and the Trial Chamber should be cautious of ruling in such a way that encourages states to violate a Defendant's rights as a means of circumventing an otherwise lawful Prosecution. The OTP acknowledges that accused persons do have the right to liberty and security of the person under international law, as recognised in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, but none of those rights have been violated in this situation. The Defendant was not deprived of his liberty except on grounds and in accordance with such procedure as are established by law, specifically, according to the Statute of the Tribunal. Furthermore, the Defendant was lawfully arrested and detained pursuant to a competent legal authority, that being the Tribunal, based on an arrest warrant, which is proof that a Judge of the Tribunal found a reasonable suspicion that the Defendant had committed the offences charged. The Defendant cannot allege that some fundamental right was violated because an arrest warrant was not addressed specifically to the FRY or that the lawful procedures of the FRY were not followed since there is no Rule that a person indicted by the Tribunal can be arrested only pursuant to the national law of the place where the person is located. In the Dokmanovic case, that Trial Chamber noted, in examining Articles 19 and 20 of the Tribunal Statute, that as long as a valid arrest warrant has been issued by the Tribunal, regardless of who may have been provided with copies, the accused may then be validly arrested in a state by an international authority, even if that state is itself unaware and does not participate in the arrest. Not only is it immaterial whether or not an arrest warrant was expressly extended to the FRY, but upon reviewing the long history of noncompliance by the FRY, the Trial Chamber in the Dokmanovic case noted that utilisation of the procedure for arrest contemplated by Rule 55 would have been futile. We contend the same is true here. In this case, valid arrest warrants were issued, thus all states were authorised to detain Mr. Todorovic for transfer to the Tribunal whether or not they had received their own copy of the arrest warrant. In fact, it must be remembered that states have certain obligations under the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, I don't know if you are going to be very much longer, but would you have an eye on the clock, please, and if you could summarise what else you have got to say? Bear in mind that we have had your fairly lengthy written submissions and we have read those.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't have that much more. Thank you. We would remind this Tribunal that the states have certain obligations under the Tribunal Statute and Rules, specifically Rules 55, 56, and 57, to make an arrest. An arrest warrant imposes a binding legal obligation on the addressee state to arrest and surrender the relevant accused. Failure to execute the arrest must be reported and explained pursuant to Article 29 and may entail adverse consequences for the state in question. Given this lawful authority, the arrest of the accused, even if it occurred in a state that is not the addressee of an arrest warrant, cannot be considered arbitrary or a violation of the accused's right to liberty and security of a person. Finally, there are compelling reasons of public policy and operational necessity for not requiring the disclosure of further information as to precisely how the accused is taken into custody. Such information will add little or nothing to assist the Chamber to arrive at its decision but will severely compromise the prospects of future arrests and will place lives at risk. The Prosecutor regards protection of those interests as being of paramount importance. When determining what are the appropriate requirements of a fair trial, the Tribunal must do so within the context of its own unique legal framework and must take account of the peculiarities and difficulties of proceeding before the Tribunal. The reality is that certain states which are under a positive legal obligation to surrender persons to the Tribunal have consistently failed to fulfil their obligations. The reality is also that certain states and super-state entities such as SFOR have been willing voluntarily to undertake operations to secure arrests of the accused. Such operations clearly involve serious security and other risks to the states concerned, including risks to the lives of the personnel involved. Let us not forget that in at least three arrest scenarios undertaken in recent months by SFOR, shots have been fired and two people have been killed. At least one SFOR soldier was injured. This is a very serious business involving attempts to arrest persons who have committed war crimes, the most serious offences that exist under international law. That said, it in no way means that the OTP condones any violation of international law, and we assume that SFOR will follow the law and do everything within its power to minimise the use of force. However, SFOR must be free to conduct these arrest missions in an appropriate manner considering the nature of the defendants, the locations where they are hiding, and the continuing political and military tensions in the former Yugoslavia. The desire of the states and forces concerned to maintain the strictest confidentiality and respect of the operational details of these activities is readily understandable. Any requirement by the Tribunal that such states and entities disclose such details to the Trial Chamber can be expected to lead to a withdrawal of their willingness to provide such voluntary assistance. This would be contrary to the interests of the fulfilment of the Tribunal's mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you say or submit that if we made the order which is sought by the Defence, that is, an order for discovery and disclosure of all details concerning the arrest, that that would be the effect of the order, as you have just described it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: We suggest, Mr. President, that SFOR and the police forces of the states involved in arresting the indictees feel that disclosing details of their operational orders, their means and methods of operating in the field, how they undertake and conduct their arrest operations, for purposes of security and confidentiality, to protect the lives of their personnel as well as all the different people that may be working with them, would seriously jeopardise their ability to conduct these arrests, and we have been informed that serious consideration would be given as to whether or not such action would be continued. I cannot state definitively that that will happen, but we have been informed that serious concerns are shared by SFOR and other states concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. Paterson, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The point that you have just made regarding SFOR, the stabilisation force, are already contained in your written document that has been given to us and that is quite well-argued. You are going a little further by saying that if we insist on the withdrawal of the indictment by the Office of the Prosecution, that this should not be considered. The problem of SFOR is not being raised here as well as the problem of the responsibility of states. What we are concerned with, as in the case of Dokmanovic which is quoted from abundantly, are two points: The first is to see whether there was any kind of collusion between the Office of the Prosecutor or any other personnel of the Tribunal, any member of the Tribunal, in any kind of unlawful activity. You told us in your written document and in your response, you said "No," your answer was "No," and I assume that you still insist on that negative answer. That is the first question that interests us here. Have you told us the following in your written document and also in your oral submission? Now, we heard talk of this arrest on the 27th of September when SFOR called us to say that somebody has been arrested, come and take him over, and we applied the procedure envisaged by the Tribunal, that is, Rule 59, et cetera. Are you confirming that, that the Office of the Prosecutor acted in this way? because that is what is important. Everything else regarding the conduct of an international force or the conduct of a state is not within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. That is the first point I wish to make. The second -- I think this point is clear -- that is, was there any violation of the rights of the accused which are guaranteed, that is true, by the International Covenants on Human Rights and the European Human Rights Convention and other international documents? Was there an arbitrary arrest in violation of the rights of the person, that is, did we not respect the legal documents and the legal proceedings prior to an arrest? You have just told us that everything was done in accordance with the Rules. There was an indictment, an arrest warrant, the accused was informed, and everything else was in order, even though we all know that an arrest is not always done very kindly. What we have to focus on is, was the Office of the Prosecutor involved in any kind of illegal act in the process of arrest? That is the point you should concentrate on. I would like to ask another question in the same sense to Mr. Brashich. Maybe I will come to that question later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me state, first of all, unequivocally, that the Office of the Prosecutor was in no way whatsoever involved in any unlawful activity in relation to the arrest of Stevan Todorovic. As I stated, we did not even find out that Mr. Todorovic was in custody until he was already at the air base in Tuzla under control of SFOR. We were informed, as we are in every case, that he was in custody, an investigator immediately went to the scene, advised him of his rights, followed all the Rules of the Tribunal, and then accompanied him here where he was taken into detention here at the Tribunal. That is unequivocal. We were not involved whatsoever in any wrongdoing in this case. The reason I was stressing the issue related to SFOR and any inquiry into operational matters is because Mr. Brashich, in his motion, has asked for an order for an evidentiary hearing, and in his oral argument, he detailed the sorts of things he wanted to ask if such a hearing were granted. He wanted to ask the names of witnesses, of participants, he wanted reports of U.N. forces, and he wanted to interview any agents that may have been involved. Those are all issues that we feel fall within operational matters of SFOR and should not be inquired into by this Tribunal unless there was an extremely compelling legal reason to do so, and we contend in this case there is none. That is the reason I was going into those arguments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Paterson, in fact, I asked you about them, and since the application is for an evidentiary hearing and since there is an application for disclosure of those matters, it is right for the Trial Chamber to know precisely what it is that is being asked for and precisely what the effect would be if the application were granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, I have a few questions. First, as to the question of the sufficiency of the material presented by the accused to warrant an evidentiary hearing. Your argument is that the material should at least establish a prima facie basis for that hearing. Do you have any authority for that standard prima facie, and might not the standard be satisfied by presentation of material which presents an arguable basis as to the legality as distinct from a prima facie basis? So that is the first question, whether you have any authority that prima facie is the basis, and, secondly, whether an arguable basis would not be sufficient? Secondly, as a matter of fact, you quite correctly, in my view, point to the paucity of material in the substantive motion itself, and you pointed to the fact that the only reference in that motion to material is a reference to published material in an e-mail. Have you taken account of the memorandum of law and the extent to which that information could be supplemented by what is in the memorandum of law, which provides a little more material and a little more information as to the allegations of illegality? Next, I want to turn to the question of the case law. You say that the OTP had no involvement in any illegal activities, and that, in your view, the case law establishes that in order for the Tribunal to refrain from exercising its jurisdiction, it must be shown that the illegalities taint the whole justice process, the whole justice system, but does that have to be established, no, and isn't that the purpose of the evidentiary hearing? Wouldn't the evidentiary hearing, if granted, assist in showing whether there was any connection between the OTP and the alleged abduction? You then turn to the question of sovereignty and the breach of sovereignty, and you say that even if the accused had been taken forcibly, there's no breach of state sovereignty, no breach of his rights, and I immediately made a note to ask you what about a breach of his rights under the International Covenant, Article 9(1), you did come to that, but I'm not sure how you have dealt with that, and I think the question that is raised is whether the manner in which he alleges he was taken from the former Yugoslavia, whether that would not be an arbitrary act such as to implicate the provisions of Article 9(1) of the covenant, which I presume you accept are applicable to the case as customary law. You mentioned the Dokmanovic case, but in that case, if my memory is correct, the warrants were issued under Rule 57 bis which authorise the issuance of the warrants to non-state parties. So I think that that case is at least distinguishable on that particular point. I don't believe that the warrants here were issued under 57 bis. Those are the issues I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Hopefully I can remember them and address them in the order you put them to me. First of all, as to the issue of whether or not the defendant has presented sufficient legal reasons to make out a prima facie case, our source for that standard is taken from several different sources, including the United Nations Human Rights Committee, the European Court of Human Rights, and the Inter-American Commission of Human Rights. We have detailed in our written submission, page 7, paragraph 19, the specifics of those particular provisions that lead us to the conclusion that that is a requirement, a burden that the defendant must meet in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that's in relation to the presentation of a substantive -- of a petition. I would rather think that in this case it is a little different, where what is being requested is an evidentiary hearing. I would tend to see that as being different from the instances that you've cited under the European convention and the Inter-American convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as we, I think, have detailed quite extensively in our written submission and here, we belief, for the reasons that I have specified, and I don't want to repeat myself, that the Defence has not presented legally sufficient reasons for this Tribunal to find a prima facie case has been met. It is our contention that no fundamental human rights of the defendant were violated in any way. Even if the worst case scenario, the facts as I detailed, even if all of those facts were true, it's our contention that no fundamental rights of this defendant were violated, including the fundamental rights under the International Covenant that you referred to. As a matter of fact, we would go so far as to say that the presentations made by the Defence in their motion is not even a reasonably arguable case, let alone a prima facie case. If I could go, since I have mentioned the International Covenant, to your question concerning that, we did acknowledge that certainly the defendant does have rights under the International Covenant, as well as the European Commission on Human Rights. Article 9(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights provides that "Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. No one shall be deprived of his liberty, except on such grounds and in accordance with such procedure as are established by law." It is our contention that Mr. Todorovic's liberty was taken from him in accordance with such procedure as are established by law. I have detailed that the OTP was not involved in any wrongdoing and that once we became involved, we scrupulously followed all the Rules of the Tribunal. Therefore, it is our contention that the procedures established by law were followed and that there was no violation of his rights under Article 9(1) of the International Covenant. If I recall, you also asked a question about the purpose of the evidentiary hearing would be to elicit further details regarding the OTP's involvement. As Judge Bennouna has pointed out, the issue is what was the involvement of the OTP? I have stated unequivocally that the OTP was not involved in any way. I can state that again, I can state it in other ways, but it is my contention that if an evidentiary hearing were held and the investigators who were involved were called, they would tell you the exact same thing that I have just told you. They received a phone call. They went to the air base. They accompanied him on the plane. They advised him of his rights. They followed all the Rules of Procedure. The OTP did everything it was required to do under the circumstances. We don't belief that anything more can be elicited regarding those facts in an evidentiary hearing. Finally, in regard to your reference to the Dokmanovic case, first of all, we think that those have to be distinguished and that, in that case, the OTP did admit involvement in the arrest of Mr. Dokmanovic. We did acknowledge that we were directly involved in his arrest, that we were involved in luring him to a place where he could be arrested and taken into custody. That is not the facts of this case, and we do think it can be distinguished. I don't want to repeat myself. I think I described in some detail our position regarding arrest warrants, but I respectfully contend, Your Honour, that we have argued that the whole issue of whether arrest warrants were directed to the FRY is not relevant in this matter, that the simple issuing of an arrest warrant, period, regardless of what state it is directed to, is sufficient to arrest the defendant. What would happen, Your Honour, if the defendant were to arrive at the Schiphol Airport, the authorities of the Dutch police were to discover he was at the airport, but because they did not have the arrest warrant that was directed to The Netherlands, they could not arrest Mr. Todorovic and bring him here to the Tribunal? Surely that cannot be the scenario, and it's our contention that the same situation existed in this case. I believe I've answered all of your questions. If you have any further clarifications you would like, please say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Brashich, you have a little time before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm taken aback by the position that the Prosecutor has taken. What I think the Prosecutor is saying is once Mr. Todorovic got to Tuzla and once, assuming arguendo that the representations made by the Prosecution are correct, that they followed the letter of the law, they read him his rights, and they brought him to The Hague. That's not our complaint. Our complaint goes from the time that he was abducted and brought to Tuzla because he wouldn't be in Tuzla unless illegal acts were committed. Assuming arguendo that the Prosecution had nothing to do with the abduction and learned about it only after Mr. Todorovic got to Tuzla, by their following and prosecuting Mr. Todorovic, they have adopted, ratified, gross violations of law. Now, ironically, the Prosecution said, "Why don't we leave the policing functions to the police professionals?" They're accusing Mr. Todorovic, who once was a police chief in Bosanski Samac, of gross violations of human rights. Why do we in this case with their policemen say, "Let's just leave them. They're professionals. They know what to do. They do not violate rights." Well, in my case with my client, hey, we can look and see whether his acts violated some international standards. If we can't police the police, that only a court can police the police, if you want to use it, the fruit of a poisoned tree, well, you can't just go in and effect a warrantless search and find heroin, cocaine, or whatever other substance, and then use that proof in a "fair trial." That is what Ms. Paterson wants you to do, that we are going to have a fair trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are an International Court. A kind of example you're using is the everyday example in a municipal court where defence counsel use this sort of argument. This is an International Tribunal dealing with totally different matters and a totally different sort of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour. If that be so, then I think that if this Court is going to apply the international standards, that it's going to have to find that this is a clear violation of Article 5(1) and Article 9(1). With regard to the violations of those Articles, those are the kidnapping, abduction, force, threats, conspiracy to do all of that. Again, with regard to public policy, confidentiality, if my client's rights have, in fact, been violated and if the Prosecution feels that about disclosure of their practices, we can have a confidentiality agreement. We can have closed sessions. I will force my client to sign a confidentiality agreement. I will do so also, as an officer of this court. I will not make it public, whatever I find out, but I think that will allow this Court to test whether or not the actions taken in bringing Mr. Todorovic to this Court violated any international standards. With regard to the prima facie case issue, Ms. Paterson concedes that on the very first appearance, it was clearly stated that he had been kidnapped and abducted, and that's in the record, and Mr. Neskovic, my prior lead counsel, also made that statement in the regard. With regard to the timeliness of the motions, I thought we had laid this at rest. As I made a representation to the Court the last time we were here, the motions went out on February 10th. The order, which I have reread, said that the motions have to be filed with the Court on February 10th. You didn't say February 10th at 5.30 p.m. Hague time. You didn't say 5.30 p.m. New York time. They were filed on February 10th according to the Rules. I also note, as I noted last time, that I got responding papers not on the date they were supposed to be served upon me but the next morning at 8.00, and they were delivered apparently to the Registrar's office at 8.00. So I think that Ms. Paterson's position with regard to the timeliness is not well-taken. Finally, Your Honour, I submit that the issue here is of this Court's subject matter jurisdiction. If subject matter jurisdiction is challenged, it can be challenged at any time during the proceedings, even on appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich, as you have made a large number of arguments, the first question regarding your first comment when you stated directly, without any shades or nuances, that it is up to the Office of the Prosecutor to prove that it did not act illegally, that is, that the burden of proof lies on the Office of the Prosecutor; that is the first question I should like you to answer. You said that the burden of proof, as I understood well, for this illegal act is up to the Prosecution. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, what I had said was that once an allegation had been made that this was an illegal abduction and kidnapping, then the burden of proof initially shifts to the Prosecution to show that the abduction, kidnapping, and bringing into detention was legal, totally without any question as to whether or not the Prosecutor had any involvement with it. That's a totally separate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich, you are making an allegation, and the Office of the Prosecutor has told you that they did not participate in any wrongdoing and that they have nothing to add. This is how things happened. Up to the present, you have not offered any prima facie evidence or any element which could illustrate or, rather, on which you could find such a grave allegation after all. Allow me to finish. You are making an accusation that there was a kidnapping. To speak Franglais, a kidnapping is an illegal act, and to allege that the Office of the Prosecutor committed it, which is, after all, an important international institution, but you have not supported this with any facts, and you are asking the Prosecution to prove that it acted legally and to reject an allegation that you're making. How do you wish them to do that? If you are making an oral allegation of that kind, then they can respond orally. You said they did such and such a thing, and they said, "We didn't do anything." After all, you cannot make such grave accusations without having any evidence, a priori evidence. You cannot ask us to have a hearing here in this Court to delve into an issue of which you have not given any elements. You have told us that there was a newspaper article. If all such articles were to be used to open hearings, I can assure you that a Tribunal could not function at all. Tell us, are you ready to present in this Trial Chamber some kind of presumption of proof, some kind of evidence, corroborating any wrongdoing by the Office of the Prosecutor because we are now appreciating the conduct of the Tribunal and not any other organ or state. So that is my question more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That's not one question, I've counted about 18, and which ones do you want me to address myself to specifically? With regard to elements of proof that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please focus on the question that you consider to be most relevant from your own standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: You're asking me what pertinent facts I have at this present time. I do not have any facts. That is why I'm asking for discovery and an evidentiary hearing. All I do know is that one day, September 27th, my client is sitting in Zlatibor, and forgetting the characterisation of the Prosecution that he was hiding, that he was doing that, he was sitting in Zlatibor in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then that very same day, he ends up in Tuzla, being kidnapped -- let's forget the word "kidnapped," we won't use the Franglais -- abducted by force by four individuals and somehow brought to an air base and then immediately thereafter taken to The Hague. That is all that my client knows. Now, as a trial attorney, I can draw inferences. I don't want to draw inferences without facts. I don't want to make accusations without facts. I am saying to this Chamber that I, unless I'm given discovery, cannot flesh out the accused's position. Now, this is an adversary procedure. With all of the issues that are raised, we have discovery. My client wasn't in The Hague. My client wasn't even in Tuzla until he got there. We don't know what happened. You had raised a point, Your Honour, where you had asked the Prosecutor whether, after Tuzla, there were any violations, and you are focusing on the procedures employed by the Prosecutor post-Tuzla. I'm saying it's not post-Tuzla that is the problem in this case. It's the pre-Tuzla actions by individuals we can't even name. We know that there were four individuals. We do not know their names. We do not know their nationalities. They were not in uniform. They were in civilian dress. Who were these people? That is what we want to find out. And if those actions by those four people were aided and abetted by SFOR or other, and I'm putting it, state agencies, international agencies, then a different standard applies. If there are any other questions you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) What standard, if there was an involvement of SFOR or anyone else, which standards apply? You must go to the end of your contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, according to Mr. Shen and cases that he has cited, and especially the decision in the Gibraltar case, and I'm thinking of the law report, the McNair 1956 decision, is that if it is a state action, then it's a prima facie case of violation of international law. If it's an individual who has violated municipal law, then that violation of municipal law becomes international law only if certain rights enumerated have been violated. Those are the two standards, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I want to go back to the same question I raised with the Prosecutor, that is, the question of the sufficiency of the material that you have presented to warrant the granting of an evidentiary hearing. You cited Dokmanovic, but I have with me here the motion filed in Dokmanovic, and if you have a look at it, you will see that there are two pages there devoted to the allegations by Dokmanovic as to the alleged illegalities. The question is why could not the accused here have presented something similar? The Prosecutor referred to an affidavit, but, in my view, it need not have been an affidavit but some statement as to outlining the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Perhaps that is my error, Your Honour. Being overcautious, I felt not completely comfortable with the procedures of this Court and whether or not such a statement, without a motion in limine, would, as I said, open the door, and, therefore, I thought that by raising the issues, that that would be sufficient to have the evidentiary hearing, and again, I might have erred, and if I had erred, then I would beg leave, should this Court feel it necessary, to have a signed statement, and I can have Mr. Todorovic right here in court sign the offer of proof which I have made on his behalf, and the only thing which he would have to add in handwriting was that he was carried from this field across the Drina River to the Tuzla air force base by an unknown helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Brashich. We will take the usual adjournment now and sit again at half past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have had the opportunity of considering this motion. The motion will be rejected. Reasons will be given in writing in due course. Now, the position is this, that one of our number has to leave at 5.15, so we should hear the motion, the remaining motion, before then, and two of us can deal with the Status Conference in due course. I think 40 minutes should be more than enough to deal with this motion. Once again, we have read the various pleadings, but, Mr. Brashich, it's for you to begin again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence motion to sever is very simple. Three of the defendants have made voluntary statements, and a number of the points raised take a position which is inimical to the interests of my clients. The Prosecution has now made a motion, which is now sub judice, that the Prosecution wishes to introduce into evidence the hearsay -- and I am mindful of this Court's/Trial Chamber's prior rulings or other Trial Chambers' rulings on the issue of hearsay -- that the unsworn, out-of-court statement be admitted into evidence. The three co-defendants do not have an obligation to testify at the trial of this case. Therefore, I would not be afforded the right to confront the witnesses which, in this case, all of a sudden have become the co-defendants, and to cross-examine them. For this reason, I feel that severance of my client from the proceedings should be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do any other Defence counsel want to say anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, fully respecting the reasons given by Mr. Brashich, we support those arguments, his motion, as well as the arguments he gave. We would just like to add that the nature of the charges against my client, Mr. Zaric, differ significantly from the nature and character of the criminal offences that Mr. Todorovic is charged with. First of all, I think it is important to point out, especially for Your Honours' determination, it is important to bear in mind that Mr. Zaric surrendered voluntarily and that he has already made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor and, therefore, I think that he has the right to expect that this Trial Chamber will deal with his case fairly and expeditiously, and I believe that if Mr. Todorovic remains together with the other accused, that this could have an adverse effect on my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I should like to join in the statement made by my learned friend, Mr. Pisarevic, and I too would support Mr. Brashich's motion for severance because I think the reasons have been validly argued. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, very briefly. First, my client has been here more than one year under the jurisdiction of the ICTY. Second, he's the first Bosnian Serb who has voluntarily surrendered himself to the jurisdiction of the ICTY. Third, if we follow this kind of enormous number of motions from my learned colleague here in order to protect the rights of his client, I think that we are very far from the date of trial. Fourth, this approach, with a joint case in trial, will, on a high level, violate the rights of my client. Finally, if the Prosecutor will state that, in terms of judicial economy, in terms of the budgetary restriction of the ICTY, in terms of, I would say, violation of the position and rights of witnesses, if that would be the case, after our submissions, I kindly ask this Trial Chamber not to draw any attention to the submissions because it is only a waste of time. In addition, we have a very clear situation pursuant to Rule 82(B), sub-rule B, where, if there is some conflict of interest between co-accused, having in mind the specific issue of this case, this request could be granted. In conclusion, Mr. Todorovic has some charges which are absolutely opposite from the case of our clients. The development of the Rules and spirit of the Rules of the ICTY, which are evidentially practically every day here, allows the Prosecutor to get some transcripts or some evidentiary hearing or facts from the other proceedings, or even from the same case, and I think that there is not any problem to grant this motion and, in future, to have a separate trial where, hypothetically, the Prosecutor can use some conclusions and some of the orders from, hypothetically, our part of the trial, in the second part of the trial. All other excuses and submissions from the Prosecutor's side will clearly show that the Prosecutor does not want to take care about the fairness and the expediency of trial because in many occasions before this hearing, the Prosecutor stated that they are ready for trial. So are we ready, as I stated at our last hearing. We were ready in June last year. Therefore, I again urge this Trial Chamber to grant this motion to sever the defendants and the counts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. This motion brought in relation to severance is, in our submission, a classic motion that you would normally encounter if there was to be a jury trial, and I say that because the issue relates to how the Tribunal will deal with the evidence that is said to be potentially dangerous evidence that could be dealt with. Traditionally, Your Honours are familiar with the sort of evidence, such as fleeting-glance evidence in identification cases, all the evidence of co-accused, whether it be testamentary evidence before the court or confessional evidence, and traditionally that is disposed of by way of giving special instructions to the jury, saying to the jury either this evidence is unsafe to rely upon unless it is corroborated; alternatively, that they can't rely upon it at all; or giving some special direction to the jury. How severance arises out of all that, Your Honours, is when the trial judge reaches the conclusion that he can't really be sure that the jury will either fully understand the direction that is given or, alternatively, the trial judge is uncertain that the jury will obey the instruction given. In those two circumstances, the trial judge may well reach a conclusion that it would be unsafe to allow the trial to proceed before a jury where this kind of evidence is to be admitted. So in those cases, and there are exceptional cases -- they tend to be exceptional cases -- the trial judge then says that the indictment is to be severed and there would be separate trials. Now, Your Honours, none of that applies here at all. When it comes to dealing with the evidence yourself, at the end of the day, it is for you to weigh it. You don't have to rely upon a jury to do it, you don't have to be concerned that it may be misapplied; it is you that is going to do it. If you feel that it is unsafe, if you feel that any of it needs to be corroborated, if you feel that it should be disregarded, that is entirely within your province. You don't sever the case in order to achieve that objective; you deal with it yourself and you address that problem at the time. Your Honours, the whole purpose of severing in a jury case is so that you are going to have a fresh jury. Another jury will hear the case, the evidence of the co-accused won't be heard, and so the whole purpose of severance is to allow the case to proceed before another jury, a fresh jury, as it were. Your Honours, in this jurisdiction, as was, in fact, referred to or mentioned in the Celebici decision, which is quoted in our motion, could well proceed before Your Honours. So, in fact, we could have one trial with some of the accused, and then the severed trial could come before you again. Now, what would be the purpose of that? That's not a fresh jury. Your Honours are going to hear the evidence all again. So in our submission, Your Honours, nothing would be achieved by that order. It is important, I think, Your Honours, first to appreciate the really significant difference between the prosecutions that are presented in this jurisdiction and in a national court. The general position in a national court is we proceed against one accused who is charged with an offence where the crime committed relates to something that he or she has done in order to satisfy their own ends. So those cases are generally cases involving one person for one purpose, that is their purpose, their personal, individual purpose. I'm not saying there isn't conspiracies and multiple cases, but I'm talking about the general situation. Now, in this jurisdiction, we are talking about crimes which occurred on behalf of a state or an institution such as the police, the army, a political party. So the objective of the crime, at the end of the day, is not the individual purpose. So there is that element of individuality that has been removed from the cases. In addition to that, invariably, it is carried on by multiple parties. So that all of the indictments that tend to be presented here are multiple-party indictments. If there are separate trials and individual trials or trials against persons, single persons, as there are, the reason for that is not because of issues of severance because of evidentiary matters, it is because there has been random arrests. Persons come here at one stage, they are in a multiple indictment, and they are severed out, generally, in most cases, with the support of the Prosecution or, indeed, I believe in one case, on the application of the Prosecution, and the reason for that is so the trial can take place. Otherwise, the accused would languish in prison awaiting trial for the other co-accused to arrive. So, in my submission, Your Honours, when you are looking at the issue of severance in this jurisdiction, I submit that it is very important to have regard to the nature of the offences, and I say this in support of the submission I now make, that is, that severance should be a very, very exceptional circumstance and very rarely based on an evidentiary question which is entirely in Your Honours' hands to deal with. Your Honours, I also submit that if there was severance in this case, in the case of Mr. Todorovic, that could work an injustice to him, an injustice that, in my submission, the Tribunal should not be party to. That injustice is the question of speedy trial. Now, if the indictment is severed so that he gets a separate trial, would it be fair that his trial proceeds against all the other accused in custody awaiting trial? In my submission, no, it wouldn't, and he should wait, if there is severance, and he should wait until all the trials are concluded because it is his motion, he is the one who wants a separate trial. Why should he be given precedence over other accused who are now in custody awaiting trial? That could mean -- I don't know how long that would mean, but it would be a considerable delay, I would have thought, before the Tribunal disposes of all its business so it can then turn around and deal with Mr. Todorovic's case. So I would submit that that would work a considerable injustice in terms of delay. So Your Honours, in considering this, have the issue of speedy trial versus an evidentiary question, and that is really what it boils down to, and in my submission, Your Honours, the speedy trial issue is vastly more important for Mr. Todorovic, at the end of the day, even though he may suggest to you otherwise. Another matter for this jurisdiction, Your Honours, that I say distinguishes it when it comes to considering severance is the trials themselves and the cost of the trial, which are very relevant considerations. In a national jurisdiction, your witnesses generally come from the same area, the same city; rarely do they come from another city in the same country. But even more exceptionally do they come to you from outside of the country altogether and abroad. That is a most exceptional circumstance. In this jurisdiction, Your Honour, it is the rule. It is very, very rare that we present to you evidence of witnesses who are resident in The Hague or in the Netherlands. Most people come from the former Yugoslavia or various parts of the world, from as far away as the Americas and Asia. So in our submission, Your Honours, the cost consideration, when it comes to severance, is a very real and appropriate one, and again, I use it in support of my submission that severance should be a very rare order that is given, particularly if it is based on an evidentiary question. Finally, Your Honours, I just note that this is a case where the accused have, at least in Count 1, all been charged within the one count.
